task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-06-16, in the area of defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid)):
Adhering to a suppression-conditional recommended mix predicts winning.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 54 series

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

methodological_questions: defining adherence to a conditional recommended mix from play-by-play data
testing whether adherence to recommended mix predicts winning
avoiding outcome-derived labels when defining optimal mix
handling small sample sizes in series-level analysis
accounting for opponent strength and game context
evidence_does_not_establish: Everything about this specific question remains open.
own_inferences: The 'suppression-conditional recommended mix' is a prescription that must be defined before seeing outcomes. Without a pre-existing, independently validated model of optimal defensive mixing, constructing such a model from the same data used to test the hypothesis would be a textbook outcome-derived label risk (circular reasoning).
There is no standard, widely accepted, pre-registered optimal defensive mix model for NBA play types.

The sample size is limited to 54 series. Statistical power to detect a realistic effect of adherence on series-level winning (binary outcome) is likely very low unless the effect is implausibly large.

Confounding is severe: adherence to a recommended mix may correlate with overall team quality, coaching skill, player execution ability, and opponent strength. Disentangling the effect of adherence from these confounds requires strong, partially untestable assumptions.

Measuring adherence requires mapping continuous play-by-play and play-type data to a finite set of defensive strategies, defining what constitutes a 'recommended' vs 'non-recommended' defensive action for each possession, and aggregating this into an adherence metric. This process involves many untestable measurement choices (e.g., tolerance windows, classification rules, weighting).

If the recommended mix is conditioned on game state (score, time, opponent lineup), the number of condition-specific recommendations grows quickly, leading to data sparsity and unreliable adherence estimates per condition.
Regression to the mean may generate a spurious positive association: teams that win a series may be judged post hoc as having adhered better to an outcome-derived 'optimal' mix.
uncertainties: Whether a defensible, pre-registered optimal defensive mix model exists that can be fixed before any contact with the outcome data of the test period.
Whether the play-by-play and play-type possession data contain sufficient detail and fidelity to reliably classify defensive actions into the categories required by the mix model.
Whether the 54 series provide enough variation in adherence and enough win/loss events to reach acceptable power even after defining the mix purely on prior data.

historical_effect.explanation: No historical evidence was retrieved, so the assessment relies entirely on domain reasoning about the research design, data limitations, and statistical risks.

blocking_constraints.text: The recommended mix is highly likely to be inferred from the same outcomes used to test adherence, unless an independently defined and validated optimal-mix model is available from prior, disjoint data. No such model is described.
With 54 series and a binary winning outcome, power to detect a realistic effect of an adherence metric on series wins is low unless the effect size is unrealistically large.
Team strength, opponent quality, coaching quality, and player health all influence both adherence and winning, and are nearly impossible to fully control in an observational study of this scale.

Operationalizing adherence requires classifying every defensive possession into recommended or non-recommended actions based on play-type and context; the reliability and construct validity of such a classification from available data are questionable.

prior_work.summary: No prior work was retrieved, so it is unknown whether this question has been studied before.

risks.text: If the recommended mix is learned from the same 54 series used for testing, the adherence metric will be a transformed version of the outcome, virtually guaranteeing an apparent but ungeneralizable association.
54 series with a binary outcome limit effective sample size. A minimum effect size of interest would likely require implausibly strong predictability from adherence alone.

Observed adherence to a recommended mix is heavily confounded by team and opponent quality, coaching system, and game script. A naive test would reflect those confounds rather than a causal effect of adhering.

Defining adherence from play-by-play and derived play-type data involves many researcher degrees of freedom (e.g., action categorization, temporal alignment, context conditioning), risking low inter-rater reliability and p-hacking.
A 'recommended mix' derived from league averages may mechanically correlate with winning if it encodes general defensive efficiency rather than a specific, contextual counter-strategy.
Exploratory search for the best conditioning variables and mix definition can inflate false positive rates unless multiplicity is strictly controlled, which is difficult with a single sample.
The NBA rule changes and playing style evolution over the four seasons could make a mix recommended from older seasons obsolete when tested on newer ones.

design.estimand: The effect of a team's series-level adherence to a pre-defined suppression-conditional recommended defensive mix on the probability of winning that series, adjusted for pre-series team strength and rest.
design.sample: All 54 completed playoff series. The recommended mix must be derived from a completely disjoint dataset, e.g., regular-season games from prior seasons not used in the test, or from a league-wide theoretical model with no fitting to the test data.
design.power: Assuming a logistic regression of series win on adherence, including a control for pre-series team strength (e.g., regular-season net rating difference), power would be adequate only for odds ratios above approximately 2.5 per one standard deviation of adherence, which is rarely plausible. Formal power analysis would require pilot data on adherence variance.
design.controls: Pre-series team strength (e.g., regular-season net rating, Elo rating, or point spread), rest days between games, home-court advantage, injuries to key players, and opponent's adherence to their own recommended offensive mix to isolate the defensive component.
design.falsification: 1. Replace the recommended mix with a randomized placebo mix (shuffling the recommendations across play types) and test that the placebo adherence does not predict winning. 2. Test that pre-series team strength, not adherence, is the dominant predictor in a model including both.
design.multiplicity: A single pre-registered primary analysis: logistic regression of series win on adherence with specified controls. No secondary measures or subgroup analyses are used for inference; any descriptive statistics are clearly labeled as exploratory.
design.decision_rule: Two-sided p < 0.05 for the adherence coefficient in the pre-specified model, with no adjustment because exactly one primary test is performed. The model must pass pre-registered goodness-of-fit checks and the falsification tests must not be significant.
design.data_version: All per-game files as of June 21, 2026, using play-by-play, defensive matchup, and derived play-type possession data from the NBA stats API, with a pre-registered date of data freeze and a pre-registered analysis script.
